sweep_summary: Xamtanga (xamt1239) is in the catalog as 'descriptions disagree' (Reinisch 1884 quantity-driven final/penult accent vs Teshome 2015 'accent not attested' vs Appleyard 1987a morphological accent). this search of works with stress in the title had one item, Langus et al. 2012 (JML), which Glottolog's own.bib record shows is a computerized mis-assignment (language code from the title word 'discover', description type from 'structure'); it is a closed-access psycholinguistics paper with no bearing on Xamtanga and should be dropped from the language's bibliography. Beyond the item list, Mous 2021 (already held by the project, read) carries Darmon 2015:33 - one obligatory primary accent per lexical word, mostly penultimate - which refines the conflict record but is second-hand and does not supersede Reinisch. Darmon 2015 (no open copy; HAL notice only) is the high-priority acquisition; Appleyard 1987a (Cambridge, paywalled, re-checked) is medium. Records saved and. only direct downloads were possible.

new_statements.reading: Xamtanga has obligatory culminative word stress (exactly one primary accent per lexical word), predominantly penultimate. This is a second-hand report of Darmon 2015 (first-hand fieldwork), not a first-hand statement itself; the only works with stress in the title (Langus et al. 2012) was a Glottolog computerized mis-assignment and contains nothing on Xamtanga. The Mous/Darmon line supports the existence of word accent against Teshome 2015's footnote and gives a positional generalisation (mostly penult) that neither confirms Reinisch's quantity-driven final/penult rule nor Appleyard's morphological accent; the catalog's 'descriptions disagree' classification stands, with Darmon 2015 as the source that would resolve it.

readall_conflicts: No new source was opened, so no new disagreement arises. The standing conflict recorded in the existing statement remains: the second-hand Darmon 2015:33 report (via Mous 2021 p.4: one culminative primary accent per lexical word, mostly penultimate) versus Reinisch's quantity-driven final/penult rule, Appleyard's morphological accent, and Teshome 2015's footnote doubting word accent; Darmon 2015 is the source that would resolve it and it is not openly available.

audit.recode_to: Not decidable without Darmon 2015 p.33 / Appleyard 1987a p.250. If Darmon confirms obligatory word accent 'mostly penultimate' with morphological/lexical residue, the Teshome 'no accent' leg should be demoted to a caution and the record reclassified off 'descriptions disagree' (either to Reinisch-style weight-sensitive hedged final/penult window if Darmon's conditioning is quantity-based, or to penult-default with morphological exceptions if it follows Appleyard).

(2) The deciding primary is an 1884 grammar whose author himself hedges the accent norms; the opposing leg is a literature-review footnote in a 2015 PhD with no prosody section; the third leg (Appleyard 1987a) is second-hand. (3) Glottolog lists two modern first-hand descriptions we do not hold (Appleyard 1987 BSOAS sketch; Darmon 2015 Lyon 2 PhD, 338 pp) plus Darmon 2023 (OUP handbook). sources.quote: Among the Agaw or Central Cushitic languages, Xamtanga is a stress language as it has one and only one primary accent per lexical word which falls mostly on the penultimate syllable (Darmon 2015: 33). In the other Central Cushitic languages, however, obligatoriness is not clearly attested.
sources.locator: PDF p.4 (printed running head '4 Mous'), section on stress languages, paragraph 'A number of Cushitic languages obey the criteria of stress languages'
sources.note: Second-hand (Mous carrying Darmon 2015:33): Xamtanga has obligatory, culminative word stress - exactly one primary accent per lexical word - falling mostly on the penult. Refines the catalog's 'descriptions disagree' record: it sides against Teshome 2015 fn.5 (accent not attested) on the existence of word accent, and gives a positional statement ('mostly penultimate') that differs from Reinisch 1884's quantity-driven final/penult rule and from Appleyard's 'largely a question of morphology'. Not first-hand, one sentence; Darmon 2015 itself remains unopened.
